settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The map-based overloads decode(String, Map<String,Verifier>) and decode(String, Map<String,Verifier>, Function) require a non-null verifiers map and never take the empty-verifier unsigned branch; they look up the verifier by kid and route through decode(...) which throws MissingVerifierException when parts.length == 3 and no verifier is found (JWTDecoder.java:117-143, 159-160).

For signed tokens, a verifier that does not support the header algorithm is nulled out (JWTDecoder.java:136-139) and a missing verifier causes MissingVerifierException, so alg confusion to none requires the empty-verifier varargs path.

README documents 'none (Unsecured)' as a supported algorithm and the >1.3.0 security notice references a prior validation flaw; the code at HEAD appears intended to reject alg:none when verifiers are present (throw InvalidJWTSignatureException at line 74/129 only fires when a verifier set/array is empty in the branch; with non-empty verifiers and no signature the flow reaches lines 163-166).
candidates.description: The varargs decode(String, Verifier...) path (JWTDecoder.java:65-76) treats a two-part token as unsigned and, when the caller supplies zero verifiers, returns the parsed claims directly if the token header's alg is Algorithm.none (lines 70-72). No verifier or signature is ever required on this branch. Because the varargs form is easy to call with no verifiers (e.g., a caller that assembled an empty/generic verifier list, or simply invoked decode(jwt) while expecting signature enforcement), an attacker can craft a fully attacker-controlled JWT whose header sets "alg":"none", base64url-encode arbitrary claims, append a trailing dot, and have those claims accepted as valid. The branch bypasses the verifier lookup, MissingVerifierException, and InvalidJWTSignatureException checks that normally guard signed tokens (lines 79-86 and 153-172). Note this is distinct from the alg:none acceptance that occurs only when the caller deliberately passes zero verifiers; the library provides no fail-closed default that requires a verifier.
missing_evidence: No call sites of JWTDecoder.decode(String, Verifier...) exist in this repository to demonstrate an application actually invoking it with zero verifiers; exploitability depends on external caller behavior not present here.
No evidence that a downstream application consumes the returned JWT without performing its own signature verification.

The exact conditions under which parts.length == 2 (a token ending in a bare dot) is produced by real clients versus normal three-part tokens were not traced beyond getParts (JWTDecoder.java:189-197).
preconditions: Caller invokes JWTDecoder.decode(encodedJWT) or decode(encodedJWT, varargs) with an empty verifier array/collection, while expecting the JWT to be signature-validated.
Token is two-part (header.payload.) with header alg == none, which the decoder deserializes into Algorithm.none (Header.java:33-34, Algorithm.java:58).
The application relies on the returned claims (subject, iss, aud, custom claims) for authorization or identity without an independent signature check.
candidates.title: JWTDecoder accepts unsigned JWTs with alg:none whenever no verifier is supplied (decode(String, Verifier...))

counter_evidence: base64Decode catches IllegalArgumentException and rethrows InvalidJWTException (JWTDecoder.java:145-151), and getParts throws InvalidJWTException for clearly wrong shapes (lines 196).
Objects.requireNonNull guards null encodedJWT and verifiers (lines 62-63).
There is a test asserting a malformed three-part-required input throws InvalidJWTException (JWTTest test referencing decode of a two-part none token).
candidates.description: In JWTDecoder.decode(String, Verifier...) the header is read via base64Decode(parts[0]...) at line 67 after getParts. getParts accepts parts.length == 2 only when the token ends in a bare dot (line 192) but still returns the array, so parts[1] indexing in the unsigned branch is safe. However the varargs decode path also indexes parts[1] at line 174 inside the private decode(...) and parts[2] at line 170; getParts requires length 3 or (2 and endsWith '.') and otherwise throws. The concern is the boundary handling is inconsistent: the exception type for structurally invalid input depends on which branch is reached, and index access is not uniformly guarded (e.g., parts[0] is read at line 67/123 before any length/null validation of array contents beyond getParts). This is a robustness/DoS candidate rather than a data-integrity issue.
missing_evidence: No concrete malformed input string was executed to confirm which unchecked exception is actually thrown; this remains unverified from static reading.
No evidence any caller treats the thrown exception type as a security boundary.
preconditions: Attacker can supply an arbitrary encodedJWT string to decode(...).
Input is structured so getParts returns an accepted array but a later index or Base64 decode path produces an unchecked runtime exception rather than the intended InvalidJWTException.
candidates.title: Malformed JWT input yields ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException in the verifier-array decode path instead of InvalidJWTException

counter_evidence: exp and nbf claims are enforced and throw JWTExpiredException / JWTUnavailableForProcessingException (JWTDecoder.java:176-184).
RSA keys are length-checked to >= 2048 bits (RSAVerifier.java:44-47, RSASigner.java:48-51); JWTUtils provides 32/48/64-byte SecureRandom HMAC secrets (JWTUtils.java:68-94).
Absence of aud/iss enforcement may be intentional library scope; README examples never set an expected audience.
candidates.description: The decoder validates only exp and nbf (JWTDecoder.java:174-184; JWT.java isExpired/isUnavailableForProcessing at 290-302). There is no check of the aud or iss claims, so a token issued for any audience/issuer is accepted if the signature verifies. Additionally, RSAVerifier and RSASigner enforce a 2048-bit minimum modulus (RSAVerifier.java:44-47, RSASigner.java:48-51) but HMACVerifier/HMACSigner accept an arbitrary-length secret with no minimum check (HMACVerifier.java:40-43, HMACSigner.java:40-43). This is a defense-in-depth gap: applications relying solely on the library to bind tokens to an audience/issuer, or using short HMAC secrets, may accept tokens that should be rejected.
missing_evidence: No application code in this repo to show aud/iss are left unvalidated in practice.
No configuration surface enforcing a minimum HMAC secret length exists to confirm it is omitted rather than enforced elsewhere.
preconditions: Application does not perform its own aud/iss checks after calling decode(...).
For the HMAC aspect, deployers configure a low-entropy/short secret via HMACVerifier.newVerifier(secret)/HMACSigner.newSigner(secret).
candidates.title: No audience/issuer validation and no HMAC secret-strength enforcement; RSA only enforces key length
